- Model consistently overestimates prices, especially in the early part of the forecast horizon (first 5–10 days).
- Forecasts tend to peak too early and then drop sharply, missing the true price’s gradual mean reversion or sustained trend.
- Overshoots after sharp spikes (e.g., post-75–77 range) are common, leading to overcorrection downward.
- Model underestimates the true mean price level in the later days of the forecast (last 10–15 days), suggesting a lag in adjusting to recent price behavior.
- Forecasts show strong sensitivity to recent history, but fail to account for structural shifts or policy-driven volatility (e.g., ETS auction timing, compliance deadlines).
- When the true price rises above 78–80, model tends to overreact and overshoot by 2–5 points, then corrects too late.
- Model exhibits “sticky” behavior — once a price level is reached, it resists downward movement, even when true price declines.
- Forecasts often ignore the influence of short-term volatility (e.g., auction-driven spikes) and treat price as a smooth trend.
- Mean reversion is under-predicted — model holds prices too high for too long after a spike, failing to reflect natural correction.
- Model tends to overfit recent data, especially when prices are trending upward, leading to overconfidence in upward momentum.
